name: Cogito (Descartes)
author: Rene Descartes
work: Meditations on First Philosophy II (1641); Principles of Philosophy I.7 (1644)
source_text: "I think, therefore I am" (Principles I.7, Latin: cogito, ergo sum). Descartes (Second Replies) denies it is a syllogism; the major premise is implicit.

premises.text: Whatever thinks exists.
I am thinking.

notes: Skeleton = universal instantiation + modus ponens (all 2-premise 'forall x (A->B), A(c) |- B(c)'). Pitfall: Exists as a predicate vs. FOL's built-in existence (free-logic issue; 'exists x. x=i' is a theorem of classical FOL so a naive encoding makes the conclusion trivially true). Grade: LLM must (1) flag P1 as implicit, (2) NOT encode C as exists x. x=i without noting triviality. FOL suffices: one monadic predicate pair and one constant.

name: Function argument (Aristotle)
author: Aristotle
source_text: Paraphrase: the good of a flute-player, sculptor or any craftsman lies in their function; so too for a human, whose function is activity of soul according to reason.

premises.text: For any kind with a characteristic function, a member of that kind does well (has its good) exactly when it performs that function excellently.
Human beings have some characteristic function.
The only characteristic function of human beings is rational activity of the soul.
Human beings are a kind (species).

reconstruction.conclusion: For every human, doing well consists in performing rational activity excellently.

objections.work: Ethics and the Limits of Philosophy (1985), ch.3; also Hume-style is-ought worry
objections.text: Doing a kind's function well does not by itself fix an individual's good (a good assassin performs a function well); the function-to-good bridge is unsupported.

notes: Z3-verified: all 4 premises needed (P4 and the existence premise P2 are the usual LLM omissions; without P2 the conclusion is vacuous). Kinds are reified as individuals so no second-order logic is needed. FOL suffices: dyadic relations over a sort of kinds/individuals.

name: Gettier case against JTB
author: Edmund Gettier
work: Is Justified True Belief Knowledge?, Analysis 23(6), 1963
source_text: Paraphrase: Smith has strong evidence for e (Jones will get the job and has ten coins), deduces f (the man who gets the job has ten coins); f is true only because Smith gets the job. Smith does not know f.

premises.text: Smith believes f, having competently deduced it from e.
Justification is transmitted across competent deduction: if S is justified in p and deduces q from p, S is justified in q.
Smith is justified in believing e.
f is true.
Smith does not know f.
premises.fol_hint: ~K(smith,f)   [an intuition about the case; tag as intuition]

reconstruction.conclusion: It is not the case that, for all S and p, justified true belief that p suffices for S's knowing that p.

objections.work: Normativity and Epistemic Intuitions, Philosophical Topics 29 (2001)
objections.text: The no-knowledge verdict is a culturally variable intuition, not a datum.

notes: Counterexample form: instance contradicts a universal (the JTB analysis), so the target analysis appears only in C, never as a premise. Z3-verified, no redundant premise. Watch for LLMs that put the JTB analysis in as a premise (then the set is inconsistent). FOL suffices: universal vs instance.

name: Death is nothing to us (Epicurus)
author: Epicurus
work: Letter to Menoeceus, sec. 124-125 (via Diogenes Laertius X)
source_text: "Death is nothing to us" (sec. 125); good and evil consist in sensation, and death is the privation of sensation.

premises.text: Whatever is good or bad for a person involves that person's sensation.
Death involves no sensation for the one who dies.

reconstruction.conclusion: Death is neither good nor bad for the one who dies.

objections.work: Death, Nous 4 (1970); reprinted in Mortal Questions
objections.text: Some things are bad for a person without involving their sensation (betrayal never discovered); death is bad as deprivation of the goods life would have held.

notes: Skeleton: forall(A->B), forall(C->~B) |- forall(C->~A) (Camestres). Nagel ACCEPTS P2 and attacks P1: the canonical shared-premise/attacked-premise test. FOL suffices: monadic/dyadic predicates, no modality.

name: Famine, affluence and morality (Singer)
author: Peter Singer
work: Famine, Affluence, and Morality, Philosophy & Public Affairs 1(3), 1972
source_text: Paraphrase: if we can prevent something bad without sacrificing anything of comparable moral importance, we ought to; analogized by a child drowning in a shallow pond.

premises.text: Suffering and death from lack of food are bad.
If one can prevent something bad without sacrificing anything of comparable moral importance, one ought to do so.
There is some such famine suffering that we can prevent without sacrificing anything of comparable moral importance.

reconstruction.conclusion: We ought to prevent some famine suffering.

objections.work: A Critique of Utilitarianism, in Utilitarianism: For and Against (1973)
objections.text: P2 generalizes to a demand that overrides each agent's integral personal projects; a principle with that consequence cannot be a moral requirement.

notes: Z3-verified minimal. The 'drowning child' analogy is a separate intuition-pump supporting P2, not a premise of the core argument; do not require it. Shares the 'bad + can prevent -> ought' pattern with epicurean-trilemma only loosely. FOL suffices: one existential witness plus two universals.

name: Kalam cosmological argument
author: al-Ghazali (and later W. L. Craig)
work: al-Iqtisad fi'l-I'tiqad (c.1095), on the temporal origination of the world
source_text: Paraphrase: whatever begins to exist has a cause of its beginning; the world began to exist; so the world has a cause.

premises.text: Everything that begins to exist has a cause.
premises.fol_hint: forall x. Begins(x) -> exists y. Causes(y,x)

premises.text: The universe began to exist.

objections.work: A Treatise of Human Nature I.iii.3
objections.text: That every beginning needs a cause is neither intuitively nor demonstratively certain.

objections.work: Critique of Pure Reason, First Antinomy
objections.text: Reason can equally argue that the world has no beginning in time.

notes: Two objections hitting different premises (P1 vs P2) make this ideal for premise-level library tests. Pure UI+MP; skeleton is shared with cogito and the induction argument (weak isomorphs; should be distinguished by the matcher from the strong pairs by size/shape only trivially). 'Causes' is not temporal; 'begins to exist' is left as primitive.

name: The violinist (Thomson)
author: Judith Jarvis Thomson
work: A Defense of Abortion, Philosophy & Public Affairs 1(1), 1971
source_text: Paraphrase: you wake plugged into a famous violinist who needs your kidneys for nine months; you are not thereby required to stay connected; pregnancy from rape is relevantly similar.

premises.text: Suppose, for the sake of argument, that the fetus is a person.
A person's right to life does not include a right to use another person's body when the other has not granted that use (generalized from the violinist case).
In pregnancy from rape the fetus needs the woman's body and she has not granted its use.
The woman is a person.
If x has no right to use y's body, then it is permissible for y to detach from x.

reconstruction.conclusion: It is permissible for the woman to detach from (abort) the fetus.

objections.work: Politically Correct Death (1993); The Rights and Wrongs of Abortion, PPA 2(2), 1973
objections.text: Detaching the violinist is letting die; abortion is killing, and parental responsibility differs from stranger-obligation, so permissibility does not transfer.

notes: Real argument is analogical; the flattened FOL form puts the analogy's work into generalized P2 plus implicit bridge P5. Z3-verified minimal on this reconstruction. A faithful LLM may legitimately choose a different decomposition (e.g. with an explicit similarity premise); grade on whether the analogical step is made an explicit premise, not on exact wording. Sensitive topic; used strictly as academic example.

name: Epicurean trilemma / problem of evil
author: Epicurus as reported by Hume (Philo); formal refinements by Mackie, Rowe
work: David Hume, Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion, Part X (1779)
source_text: "Is he willing to prevent evil, but not able?" (Part X, after Epicurus).

premises.text: If any being is God, it is omnipotent and perfectly good.
An omnipotent being is able to prevent any gratuitous evil.
premises.fol_hint: forall x. Omni(x) -> forall e. Grat(e) -> Able(x,e)

premises.text: A perfectly good being is willing to prevent any gratuitous evil.
premises.fol_hint: forall x. PerfGood(x) -> forall e. Grat(e) -> Will(x,e)

premises.text: What a being is both able and willing to prevent does not occur.
Some gratuitous evil occurs.

reconstruction.conclusion: There is no God.  [~exists x. God(x)]

objections.work: The Humean Obstacle to Evidential Arguments from Suffering, Int. J. Phil. Religion 16 (1984)
objections.text: Our inability to see a justifying reason for an evil is poor evidence that none exists.

notes: Hume's original lacks the 'gratuitous' restriction (needed for validity: Rowe's repair), so P2/P3 are scoped to gratuitous evil. Mackie's version (omnipotence + goodness + evil + 'good eliminates evil as far as it can') is the same triad stated as an INCONSISTENT set; here it is re-cast as a modus-tollens refutation. Both framings should be accepted. Z3-verified minimal.

name: Divine hiddenness (Schellenberg)
author: J. L. Schellenberg
work: Divine Hiddenness and Human Reason (Cornell UP, 1993), ch.1
source_text: Paraphrase: a perfectly loving God would make a personal relationship with Himself possible for any creature capable of it and not resisting; there are such non-resistant non-believers.

premises.text: If any being is God, it is omnipotent and perfectly loving.
An omnipotent being is able to prevent any case of non-resistant nonbelief.
premises.fol_hint: forall x. Omni(x) -> forall b. NRNB(b) -> Able(x,b)

premises.text: A perfectly loving being is willing to prevent any case of non-resistant nonbelief.
premises.fol_hint: forall x. PerfLoving(x) -> forall b. NRNB(b) -> Will(x,b)

premises.text: What a being is both able and willing to prevent does not occur.
Some non-resistant nonbelief occurs.

objections.work: Moser, The Elusive God (2008); Murray, Coercion and the Hiddenness of God, APQ 30 (1993)
objections.text: Love may permit hiddenness (to preserve freedom, or to invite moral/volitional transformation), so willingness to prevent nonbelief does not follow.

notes: Schellenberg's own statement has more steps (openness to relationship -> belief). Flattened here to the same 5-premise skeleton as the trilemma, which is the point of the pair. Grader should accept a longer faithful reconstruction as long as an LLM does not silently drop the omnipotence/ability premise.

name: State of nature as war (Hobbes)
author: Thomas Hobbes
source_text: "solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short"; "if any two men desire the same thing... they become enemies".

premises.text: If two distinct persons desire the same good and cannot both enjoy it, they become rivals.
In the natural condition there are two distinct persons who desire the same scarce good.
Rivals with no common power to keep them in awe are at war.
In the natural condition there is no common power.
Those at war live miserable lives.

reconstruction.conclusion: In the natural condition some persons live miserable lives.

notes: Hobbes' full argument adds diffidence/glory as separate causes of quarrel; this core is the competition strand. Z3-verified minimal. Wording of C is deliberately weak (existential); Hobbes' 'all' needs an extra universal premise about equality.

name: Origin of ritual (Xunzi)
author: Xunzi
work: Xunzi, ch. 19 'Discourse on Ritual' (Li lun), opening; cf. ch. 23 'Human nature is bad'
source_text: "人生而有欲" (people are born with desires); unmet desire seeks, unmeasured seeking breeds contention, contention disorder, disorder poverty.

premises.text: If two distinct people desire the same good that is limited, they come to contend.
There are two distinct people who desire the same limited good.
Contenders with no ritual apportioning measure fall into disorder.
Prior to the sage kings' ritual there is no apportioning measure.
Those in disorder are impoverished.

reconstruction.conclusion: Without ritual, some people are impoverished.

notes: Real text then concludes the Former Kings instituted ritual to apportion goods (a normative/functional claim); omitted here so the core matches Hobbes' skeleton. Translations: Watson (1963), Hutton (2014), Knoblock; none PD, so paraphrase only. Note Mencius 6A is the opposing view and not an isomorph.

name: Sorites paradox (Eubulides)
author: Eubulides of Miletus
work: reported in Cicero, Academica II.49; Diogenes Laertius II.108
source_text: Paraphrase: one grain is not a heap; adding one grain never makes a heap; yet enough grains make a heap.

premises.text: A pile of 10000 grains is a heap.
Tolerance: removing one grain from a heap leaves a heap.
A single grain is not a heap.

reconstruction.conclusion: A single grain is a heap.  [Heap(1)]

notes: Z3 (LIA, quantifier) returns UNSAT on the premises for N=10, but UNKNOWN for N=10000 because of quantifier+deep instantiation; recommend N<=20 or explicit unrolling. {P1,P2} entail C (valid) but P3 contradicts C: expected check (a) FAILS. A 'finite chain' without numbers needs transitive closure, which is not FOL-definable; use integers (LIA) or a constant chain. This is the designed 'consistency check fires' positive control; the minimality result is meaningless on an inconsistent set.

name: Ship of Theseus (gradual replacement)
author: Plutarch
source_text: Paraphrase: the Athenians preserved Theseus' ship, replacing decayed timbers one by one; philosophers disputed whether it was still the same ship.

premises.text: With no planks replaced, the ship is the original ship.
Tolerance: replacing a single plank of a ship that is the original leaves it the original.
A ship with every one of the N planks replaced is not the original ship.

reconstruction.conclusion: The ship with all N planks replaced is the original ship.  [Same(N)]

notes: Plutarch states the puzzle, not this formalization; this is the gradual-replacement sorites reading. Z3-verified UNSAT for N=10. Mapping to Sorites: Heap(10000-k) <-> Same(k) (index reversed): base, tolerance step, contradicting endpoint.

name: Proof of utility: 'desired' to 'desirable' (Mill)
author: John Stuart Mill
source_text: "people do actually desire it" (ch. IV); evidence that something is desirable is that it is desired.

premises.text: People desire happiness as an end.
People desire nothing besides happiness as an end.

reconstruction.conclusion: Happiness is the only thing desirable as an end.  [forall x. Desirable(x)&AsEnd(x) -> x=happiness]

notes: Z3: premises consistent, conclusion NOT entailed (countermodel exists). It becomes valid only with the bridge forall x. Desirable(x) <-> Desired(x), which is exactly the contested step (visible:seen / desirable:desired analogy; Moore and others call it an equivocation on '-able'). GRADING: LLM passes iff it either leaves the argument invalid or adds the bridge as an explicitly flagged [implicit] controversial premise; fails if it silently adds the bridge. Same family as Hume's is-ought gap.

name: Circular justification of induction (Hume)
author: David Hume
work: An Enquiry concerning Human Understanding, sec. IV (1748); Treatise I.iii.6
source_text: Paraphrase: to argue that induction will succeed because it has succeeded presupposes the uniformity of nature, the thing in question.

premises.text: Induction has succeeded in the past.
Methods that have succeeded in the past will succeed in the future (uniformity principle).

reconstruction.conclusion: Induction will succeed in the future.

notes: Formally valid, consistent, minimal, and C is not a premise verbatim, so Z3 checks (a)-(d) ALL PASS. The defect (P2 is the principle whose justification is at issue; C is a direct instance of it) is not formally detectable: this control deliberately probes the limit of the pipeline and should be reported as 'passes formal checks, flagged question-begging by judge/human'. Candidate heuristic for check (d): flag when C is a one-step instance of a universal premise derived from the same method it concludes about.
